choices.text: terraform plan -refresh-only, to confirm that no one changed the live resources outside Terraform
terraform apply on a plan file produced earlier, to prove that the plan can be executed
terraform plan with the default refresh, to show reviewers the changes against the live resources
terraform init -backend=false followed by terraform validate, to catch syntax and type errors
terraform fmt -check -recursive, to fail the build when any file is not in canonical style

stem: A pipeline step runs terraform fmt -check in the repository root. It passes, yet a module in modules/network/ is badly formatted and reaches main. What change makes the step catch it?

choices.text: Run terraform validate first, because validation also enforces canonical formatting of every file in all modules
Add -recursive, because by default fmt processes only the current directory unless told to descend into subdirectories
Add -write=false, because without it the command silently reformats the files and then reports success
Add -diff, because the exit status becomes non-zero whenever a diff would be produced for any nested file

stem: A pipeline's validate stage passes for a change that sets instance_type to a value no provider API accepts, and the plan stage fails later. What explains the gap?

choices.text: validate was run without -var-file, so every variable was null and the invalid instance type was never evaluated
validate is limited to the root module and skips child modules, which is where the instance type was set
validate checks syntax and internal consistency only, not remote services, so accepted values of provider APIs are not tested
validate runs against the backend state and aborts only when the state holds a resource with a conflicting attribute

stem: Two CI jobs run on separate runners: a plan job writes tfplan and uploads it, and an apply job downloads it later. Which TWO statements about handling that artifact are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The apply job must run terraform init with the same lock file and Terraform version, since the plan file does not carry providers
The apply job needs -auto-approve, because a saved plan otherwise waits for an interactive confirmation prompt
The file is a standard JSON document, so reviewers can safely grep it for secrets and then share it on a public bucket for audit

The file holds the full configuration and variable values, so sensitive values sit in cleartext and it needs protected storage

stem: A pipeline plans on merge, a reviewer approves, and a later job runs terraform apply -auto-approve with a fresh plan. Last week the apply deleted a database that the reviewed plan did not mention. Which change best closes the gap?

choices.text: Apply the exact plan file that the reviewer saw, using terraform apply tfplan after the approval gate
Add -refresh=false to the apply, so the apply cannot notice new differences in live resources
Require two reviewers on the pull request, so that a second person also reads the plan output once
Run the plan twice before approval and compare the outputs, then continue with the second one

stem: A contributor opens a pull request from a fork of the company repository, and the HCP Terraform workspace connected to the repository shows no speculative plan. Pull requests from internal branches do get one. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Speculative plans start only after the pull request has been merged, since HCP Terraform needs the final destination contents
Speculative plans require the contributor to hold the apply permission in the workspace before HCP Terraform will start a run
HCP Terraform does not run speculative plans for pull requests that come from forks, to avoid running untrusted code
The fork has its own copy of the workspace variables, so the plan is queued in a different organization

stem: After a team adds -detailed-exitcode to its plan step, the pipeline starts failing on every run that has pending changes, though the plans are valid. What explains this?

choices.text: The flag makes Terraform return 1 for a non-empty plan, which signals a partial failure that the job must retry automatically
The flag adds an interactive prompt, which cannot be answered in CI and therefore aborts the step
The flag requires -out, and without a saved plan file the command ends with an unspecified error status

stem: A CI job runs terraform apply -input=false with no plan file and no -auto-approve. It ends without changing anything and reports a failure. What is the cause and the usual fix?

choices.text: The flag makes apply run in refresh-only mode, so the job only updates state and must switch to the default mode to see changes
Input is disabled, so Terraform cannot ask for approval and assumes none; apply a saved plan instead
The flag forces plan -out to a default file, and apply fails because it cannot find that file
The job lacks -lock=false, and the lock held by the previous job cannot be released without the flag

stem: An API-driven pipeline creates runs with the save-plan option on a workspace where auto-apply is enabled. Plans finish, but no run ever applies until a person confirms it. What explains the behavior?

choices.text: The workspace is in speculative mode, so none of the plans can be applied by anyone in the organization
Auto-apply needs a policy check, and runs without a policy set attached are held until confirmed
Auto-apply works only for runs started from the UI, so API runs always need confirmation regardless of options
Saved plan runs are never auto-applied, even when the workspace enables auto-apply; they apply only after confirmation

stem: A team runs a web tier on two identical stacks, blue and green, behind one load balancer. They want the cutover and the rollback to be a small, low-risk apply. Which design fits?

choices.text: Define a green stack only when releasing and delete it right afterwards, with the previous blue stack found by tags
Destroy the blue stack in the same apply that creates the green stack, using create_before_destroy on every resource
Keep both stacks defined and switch traffic with one variable such as active_color that only changes the listener's target
Use one stack and change its AMI in place, then rely on terraform apply -replace on the instances to roll back if monitoring complains

stem: A team wants a canary release: 5 percent of traffic to the new version, then 25, then 100. What does a Terraform-based design need to supply that Terraform does not do on its own?

choices.text: A pipeline gate between applies that checks metrics and decides whether the weight variable moves on
A single apply with count increasing by one each minute so that the weight grows continuously while it runs
A lifecycle setting that makes the provider observe error rates and revert the weight when failures increase
A provisioner on the listener that sleeps and raises the weight on a timer with no external check of application health

stem: A change to the AMI would replace all twelve instances of one resource in a single apply, and the service cannot lose them together. Which approach gives a batched rollout with plain Terraform?

choices.text: Use -target on the whole resource block so that Terraform processes only a subset of the instances at a time
Split the instances into groups keyed in a for_each map and roll the new AMI through one group per apply
Set -parallelism=1 on the apply so that the instances are replaced one after another within the single run
Add replace_triggered_by to every instance so that they take turns being replaced in a safe sequence

stem: A company promotes changes from dev to staging to prod. Which practice best keeps the three environments comparable?

choices.text: Keep a long-lived Git branch per environment, and cherry-pick fixes between the branches whenever somebody remembers to do it
Promote the same commit or module version tag through each environment, differing only in per-environment variable values
Copy the production directory into dev when needed, and edit the copy to remove the expensive resources
Let each environment pin the module to its own latest main branch commit so that each stays current

stem: In HCP Terraform, workspace app-staging has a run trigger from app-dev. A run in dev applies successfully; a run is queued in staging but then waits and does not apply. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Runs started by run triggers do not auto-apply unless the separate Auto-apply run triggers setting is enabled
The staging workspace needs the same name as the source workspace, otherwise queued runs are held until renamed
Run triggers only copy state from the source workspace and never start runs, so a person must start staging manually

stem: A team wants a short-lived preview environment for every pull request, built from the same configuration, and each one must be destroyable without affecting staging or the other previews. Which design fits?

choices.text: Keep one shared state, add a map entry per pull request in a tfvars file, and remove the entry when the pull request closes so that the next apply cleans up
Reuse the staging state and use -target on the new resources at apply, then target the same addresses with a destroy when the review ends
Apply each preview into the staging state, and on close run terraform state rm for its resources so that Terraform stops tracking them

stem: Which TWO statements accurately describe how HCP Terraform dynamic provider credentials work? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The token contains the cloud credentials themselves, encrypted so that only the cloud platform can open it
The same temporary credentials are reused by every run in the workspace until they expire, to avoid extra token requests

HCP Terraform stores a long-lived cloud access key per workspace and rotates it on a schedule you configure in the trust policy

stem: A platform team creates the AWS role trust policy for HCP Terraform with one condition on the token's aud claim and nothing on sub. A reviewer says the setup is unsafe. Why?

choices.text: The trust policy applies only to the plan phase, so apply tokens would be blocked by the missing condition
The aud claim is secret, so storing it in the trust policy discloses the audience to every user who can read the role

stem: Plans in one workspace must be read-only against AWS, while applies need write access. How should the dynamic credentials be set up?

Set TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH to plan on the workspace, so the apply phase falls back to a separate default identity
Create one broad role, and use TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN, because the role used for plans is limited automatically by Terraform
Create one role and add an IAM condition that denies writes whenever the command line contains the word plan

stem: Forty workspaces in one project should share a single AWS role through dynamic credentials. Which TWO actions are needed? (Select TWO)

Replace the sub condition by a wildcard for the entire organization so that new workspaces work without trust policy changes

Copy the same two environment variables into each workspace by hand, since variable sets cannot hold environment variables
Write the role's trust policy sub condition with StringLike and a pattern that wildcards the workspace and run phase within the project

stem: With Azure dynamic credentials, plans work but every apply fails to authenticate, although the same service principal is configured in the workspace. What is the likely cause?

Federated credentials match the subject as a direct string, and only the one for run_phase:plan exists, not the apply one

stem: A workspace uses dynamic credentials for a default AWS configuration. The team adds a second account via tagged variables such as TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN_PROD and declares the tfc_aws_dynamic_credentials variable. Now the default provider no longer authenticates. What was missed?

stem: Dynamic AWS credentials are enabled in a workspace, but runs still act as an old IAM user. The AWS provider block sets access_key and secret_key from variables. What should the team do?

stem: A company on Terraform Enterprise wants cloud credentials for runs but will not expose its instance's OIDC metadata endpoints to the public internet. Which approach does the HCP Terraform documentation describe for this?

Native OIDC dynamic credentials with the cloud provider, which needs public metadata endpoints for the cloud to verify the tokens
